regions.text: Today is a day for mourning and
regions.explanation: From 10.61s to 11.88s (“Today is a day for mourning and”), articulation rate was 7.09 syll/s against 5.06 syll/s in the reference (+40%); that is 1.6× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Faster articulation compresses the stressed syllables and the micro-pauses listeners use to segment phrases, so key words lose emphasis and comprehension drops. Fix: Slow to the reference pace here and let the pauses between clauses breathe.

From 12.77s to 14.12s (“Nancy and I are”), articulation rate slowed to 3.70 syll/s against 6.02 syll/s in the reference (-39%); that is 1.5× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Stretched words without matching emphasis read as hesitation and dilute the rhythm of the phrase; the audience's attention drifts between content words. Fix: Tighten these words to the reference pace; keep length only on the stressed word.

A long silence where the reference has none - especially mid-phrase - breaks the syntactic unit and signals lost place rather than deliberate emphasis. Fix: Keep this phrase in one breath; pause at the punctuation instead.

regions.text: Seven, were aware of the dangers, but
regions.explanation: From 42.70s to 44.86s (“Seven, were aware of the dangers, but”), 2 pause(s) at punctuation shrank from 215 ms to 15 ms on average. Pauses at punctuation mark the end of an idea and give the audience time to absorb it; running through them merges separate thoughts into one stream. Fix: Hold a clear pause at each punctuation mark, about as long as the reference.
